Imagine sending a message
from the surface of
a theoretical ocean planet
that orbits a giant
black hole.
Imagine standing on this
world.
Your home is not
drifting through calm space.
It is racing around
the black hole at
roughly half the speed
of light or more,
just to stay in orbit.
Your slowed time has
two causes.
The black hole's gravity
slows clocks, and your
enormous orbital speed
adds ordinary time dilation
from special relativity
on top.
Together, these two effects
stretch time by a
factor of tens of thousands.
Now suppose you want
to call home.
When light climbs out
of a gravity well,
it loses energy.
This is gravitational
redshift.
Since light cannot slow
down, it loses energy
by stretching to longer
wavelengths.
With our factor of
roughly sixty-seven
thousand, blue light from
the surface would arrive
as microwaves a few
centimeters long.
And if you say
a single word,
one second of your
voice, that signal is
stretched to last about
eighteen and a half hours.
Messages coming down the
well are the reverse.
Light from the sky
above you would be
blueshifted, squeezed into
X-rays and gamma rays.
Decades of news broadcasts,
farewells and tragedies
would pour onto your
screens in a blizzard
of data, fast-forwarded
roughly sixty-seven thousand
times.
If you could look
up from the surface,
the sky would be eerie.
The universe outside this
gravitational canyon is
not moving at your pace.
It is living and
dying at high speed.
Stars would streak across
the sky.
Any supernova in view
would flare and fade
within minutes.
You would be sitting
in a natural time
machine, anchored to the
present while the rest
of the universe races
into the future.
But would you feel
your own time slowing?
Absolutely not.
In relativity, your own
clock always ticks at
one second per second,
as measured by you.
Your heart would not
pump sluggishly, and your
thoughts would not drag.
You would breathe,
feel fear, and check
your wristwatch, completely
unaware of your detachment
until you compared notes
with the outside world.
Time is not a river.
It is a landscape.
